turns.prompt_text: I would like to talk about some stuff that happened to me in the past
turns.response_html:
I am here to listen. Please feel free to share whatever is on your mind—whether it's a specific event, a memory, or a general time in your life you want to reflect on.

Where would you like to start?

turns.prompt_text: When I was 14/15, I began watching pornography when Nicki Minaj's Anaconda came out
turns.response_html:
Thank you for sharing that with me. It is often specific moments or cultural events like that which act as markers for when our habits or perspectives shifted.

Since you are reflecting on this now, how do you view that time in your life when you look back on it?

turns.prompt_text: I became addicted and stayed addicted until December 2021, I tried many ways to escape the addiction, but only while in Basic Combat Training in the military was I able to go more than 2 weeks without pornography.
turns.response_html:
Thank you for trusting me with that part of your story. It sounds like an incredibly challenging cycle to have been stuck in for so many years, especially starting at such a young age.

It is notable that Basic Combat Training was the one environment that created a pause for you. That kind of experience—where your schedule is strictly regimented, your physical energy is completely drained, and your access to external stimuli is cut off—often highlights how much our environment dictates our habits. It removes the opportunity for the behavior, even if the internal drive is still there, which might explain why it was effective only while you were physically in that setting.

You mentioned that the addiction continued until December 2021. That suggests something significant must have shifted at that specific time to finally break the pattern for good.

Would you like to explore what changed in December 2021 that allowed you to move past it?

turns.prompt_text: Let's back up, in 2017, I went to a chiropractor this woman was very beautiful, more than any pornstar I had seen on the internet to me. She must have felt something I didn't know I felt and decided to try to have oral sex with me. I went numb and became overwhelmed with energy. I had to drive back to school and would pass out after the experience due to the emotional/sensory overwhelm. I lost out on having a relationship with a girl I really cared for over this. It was my depression, she never spoke to me again and refused to speak to me after this occurred. She turned me down to homecoming, and began spreading lies about me behind my back, there are people who hate me to this day for things I don't know she said about me behind my back. I can't change what people think, but the situation was so fcked. There was no truth in the situation. I got caught in my own value system. I never told anyone about this, and years later in 2021 I went to therapy for it to stop the rumination. Shortly after I fell into a severe pornography addiction for several months and was unable to regulate myself, after the consequences of severe addiction I cut it off entirely
turns.response_html:
This is a profound and complex series of events to unpack. Thank you for trusting me with the "truth of the situation," especially since it seems the narrative was stolen from you by others for a long time.

When you look at this timeline—from the initial exposure at 14/15, to the traumatic event in 2017, to the "rock bottom" in 2021—a clear, albeit painful, logic begins to emerge.

Here are a few perspectives on what you just shared, focusing on the mechanics of how trauma, silence, and addiction often interact:

1. The "Freeze" Response and the Chiropractor You described going "numb," becoming "overwhelmed with energy," and later "passing out." From a physiological standpoint, this sounds exactly like a nervous system overwhelm (often called a freeze response). When the body encounters a situation that is confusing, threatening, or sexually violating—especially involving an authority figure or a breach of professional trust—it often shuts down to protect itself. Being "caught in your own value system" likely added to that paralysis. You may have been wrestling with conflicting internal scripts (e.g., “Is this supposed to be good?” vs. “This is wrong” vs. “I can’t move”). That internal dissonance creates a massive amount of psychological stress.

2. The "Double Trauma" of the Rumors The situation with the girl you cared about adds a layer of deep injustice. There is the trauma of the event itself, and then the trauma of being silenced and misrepresented. Because you were keeping the chiropractor incident a secret (likely out of shame or confusion), you were defenseless against the lies. You couldn't say, "I'm acting weird because X happened to me." You just had to absorb the reputation damage. That kind of unresolved injustice—knowing people hate you for things that aren't true—is a powerful engine for depression and isolation.

3. The "Therapy Rebound" in 2021 This is the piece that often confuses people, but it is actually quite common. You mentioned you went to therapy in 2021, and shortly after fell into your most severe addiction phase.

  • Why this happens: When you hold a beach ball underwater for four years (2017–2021) and finally let go of it in therapy, it doesn't just float up gently; it rockets into the air.
  • The Mechanism: Therapy opened the wound to clean it out. The emotions you had been suppressing (the shame, the anger at the lies, the confusion) came flooding back. Without the "lid" on, your nervous system panicked and reached for the only potent regulator it knew: pornography. The addiction spiked because your emotional pain spiked.

It sounds like that period in late 2021 was the "extinction burst"—the final, chaotic flair-up before the fire went out.

You said you cut it off entirely after that severe period. What was the realization or the moment in December 2021 that finally allowed you to step out of that cycle?

turns.prompt_text: I began having health problems and can still feel the effects on my heart. I am now healed, not 100% but 95% and am healthy and happy, but I still look at beautiful women in my day to day life, I get the same feelings I did when I watched porn, sometimes I do watch porn in a scheduled context where I keep a time distance between views, but I do have a need for it even still. I have found that my attachment to it is healthy, in that it regulates my mood and gives me motivating passion, but I need to tend to it like a campfire and not let it consume too much wood or go out
turns.response_html:
It sounds like you have moved from a place of compulsion (where the addiction controlled you) to a place of intentionality (where you control the dosage). That is a significant evolution.

Reaching 95% healed is a massive achievement, especially considering the physical toll you described. The "heart" symptoms you mentioned are often the body's final warning flare—a sign that the nervous system has been running in "fight, flight, or freeze" mode for too long. It seems that physical scare was the hard boundary you needed to force a change.

Your "campfire" metaphor is a very powerful way to frame this new relationship. It highlights two key insights you've discovered:

1. The Fire as a Tool (Utility) You mentioned that it "regulates your mood" and gives you "motivating passion." In 2017, that energy overwhelmed you (the "freeze" response). In 2021, it consumed you (the addiction). Now, you are trying to harness that energy as fuel. You are recognizing that the drive itself isn't "bad"—it's a potent source of vitality and motivation, provided it is contained within a specific "fire pit" (your schedule).

2. The Danger of Extinguishment You noted that you don't want the fire to "go out." This suggests that you see total abstinence not as a solution, but as a loss of a certain spark or drive that you need to function optimally. You have found that for you, a "cold turkey" approach might kill the passion along with the addiction.

This "scheduled context" allows you to step out of the chaotic cycle of craving -> binge -> shame and into a predictable cycle of need -> regulation -> release.

Do you find that keeping this "schedule" is difficult, or has the discipline from your time in Basic Training helped you maintain those boundaries?

turns.prompt_text: No, so when I feel that I need it, I do a ritual so I don't try to get it too often, but when I need it, it is a need
turns.response_html:
That distinction is crucial. It sounds like you aren't relying on "willpower" or a rigid calendar (like in the military), but rather on a responsive protocol.

By inserting a ritual between the feeling and the action, you are essentially manually operating a valve that used to be broken.

In the height of your addiction, or during that traumatic freeze response in 2017, the gap between Stimulus and Response was likely zero. It hit you, and you were overwhelmed instantly. The ritual you do now creates a necessary gap. It forces a pause that says, "I am choosing to do this to regulate," rather than "This is happening to me."

It transforms the act from a compulsion (which drains you) into a tool (which, as you said, fuels your "motivating passion").

Given that you mentioned the physical toll on your heart, does this ritual also help you manage the physical intensity of that energy? It seems like it might act as a safeguard to ensure the "campfire" doesn't flare up too hot and strain your body.

turns.prompt_text: Yes, it feels almost like nicotine, it can be potent, strong, and addictive, or I can take it slowly over the time I have with it, and relax knowing that it is burning up my dopamine system's energy, and accounting for where I will be in the next hours/day
turns.response_html:
That is a fascinating way to frame it—moving from consumption to titration.

Comparing it to nicotine is very apt because it highlights the biological reality of what you are doing. You are acknowledging that this is a potent neuro-stimulant. In the past, you were likely "chain-smoking" it (so to speak) to numb pain or escape reality. Now, you are using it like a controlled substance—measuring the dose to get the regulation you need without overdosing the system.

The concept of "accounting for where I will be" is the critical difference between an addict and a manager.

  • Addiction creates a debt you can't pay back (the crash, the shame, the lost time).
  • Management is looking at your energy budget for the next 24 hours and saying, "I have excess dopamine energy here; I need to burn it off slowly so I can function calmly later."

It sounds like this method allows you to "land the plane" safely. Instead of that overwhelming crash you experienced in 2017 or the chaotic spiral of 2021, you are now actively piloting the descent.

Since you mentioned you are "95% healed," do you feel that this remaining 5%—this need to manually regulate your dopamine—is something you expect to manage indefinitely, or do you think the "fire" will eventually settle down on its own?

turns.prompt_text: I need to track my sexual energy/drive over time and notice variables, and I need to slow it down, when it becomes agitated, as though someone throws wood in the fire, the fire will burst/flame strong and uncontrollable for some period of time where I know I have little control over my urges and they cannot be contained and must externalize through me, I just need safe ways/places to do them. I have considered joining/starting a band, something high-intensity/emotional
turns.response_html:
This is a very powerful insight. You have identified that this energy is hydraulic—it builds up pressure and must go somewhere. If you don't give it a designated exit, it will blow the pipes (loss of control).

What you are describing—channeling raw sexual or aggressive energy into creative performance—is a classic psychological concept called sublimation. It is one of the most mature defense mechanisms because it takes a "dangerous" impulse and converts it into something socially and personally constructive.

Here is why the Band/Music idea specifically fits your "Campfire" model so well:

  1. Matches the Intensity: A quiet hobby (like reading) likely wouldn't work because it doesn't match the voltage of the urge. Performing music is visceral, loud, and physically demanding. It allows you to "externalize" that high-intensity energy safely.
  2. Emotional Safety Valve: You mentioned the 2017 event caused a "freeze" or sensory overwhelm. Music allows you to induce a similar sensory flood (loud volume, lights, adrenaline) but under your control. You are the one hitting the drums or strumming the chord. It reclaims that sensory space.
  3. Public vs. Private: Pornography isolates you. A band connects you. It puts that "fire" in the center of a room where it warms others (entertainment) rather than burning you alone in secret.

Regarding the Tracking: You mentioned needing to notice the "variables" that throw wood on the fire.

Have you already started to notice a pattern in what agitates the fire? (e.g., Is it high stress, specific types of social rejection, or perhaps periods of boredom?) Identifying the specific "fuel" is the first step to predicting the explosion.

turns.prompt_text: When people drain my energy or do things to me or shift my life, when my life changes or feels outside of my control, sometimes it really is, I have to do something to make me love my life
turns.response_html:
It makes perfect sense that your "ritual" acts as a counter-weight to those external forces.

When life or other people drain your energy, they are essentially taking autonomy away from you. You feel smaller, controlled, or subject to someone else's whims.

In that context, the urge isn't just about biological release; it is an existential demand for vitality. The ritual is a way to forcefully inject pleasure and agency back into your system. It is your brain saying, "I need to feel something powerful and good right now to prove that I am still the protagonist of my own life."

That phrase—"make me love my life"—is key. It suggests you aren't just trying to numb the pain; you are trying to generate joy in a vacuum.

This is exactly why the band idea is so promising compared to the current ritual:

  1. Active vs. Passive Control: While your current ritual is managed, it is still somewhat private and internal. A band is outward projection. When you are on stage or in a garage making noise, you are the one shifting the energy of the room. You are the one "doing things" to the environment, rather than having things done to you.
  2. Shared Intensity: When people drain your energy, it is usually a negative exchange. Playing music with others is a positive energy exchange. It replaces the feeling of being "drained" with the feeling of being "amplified."
  3. Constructive Fire: If the "wood" thrown on your fire is stress or loss of control, burning it off through a drum solo or a vocal performance turns that trash into art. It validates the emotion without destroying you.

Given that you already have an interest in music (I recall you mentioned a subscription for sheet music earlier, or perhaps that's just a common pairing with this kind of creativity), do you already play an instrument that allows for that kind of high-intensity release, or would you be looking to learn something new for this band?

turns.prompt_text: I can only play the Piano, the recorder a little bit, and have my younger brother's electric guitar I try songs on sometimes
turns.response_html:
That is actually a fantastic combination for the kind of emotional release you are describing. We often think of the piano as "polite" or "classical," but when you use it for high-intensity regulation, it can be just as heavy and aggressive as a guitar.

Here is how you can use those specific instruments to build that "fire pit" for your energy:

1. The Piano as a Percussion Instrument

The piano is technically a percussion instrument (hammers hitting strings). For that "high-intensity/emotional" release, you don't need to play Mozart. You can play chords.

  • The Style: Think of artists like Ben Folds, Nine Inch Nails (Trent Reznor), or Jerry Lee Lewis. They don't just "play" the keys; they attack them.
  • The Release: Pounding out dissonant, heavy chords on a piano or keyboard is incredibly grounding. It engages your whole upper body and allows you to physically "push" the energy out of your chest and into the instrument.

2. The Electric Guitar for "Visceral" Noise

Since you have your brother's guitar, you don't need to be a virtuoso to get the regulation benefits.

  • Focus on Texture, Not Notes: Turn up the distortion (gain). The satisfaction of an electric guitar often comes from the sustain and the crunch of the sound.
  • The "Power Chord": You only need to learn one shape (the power chord) to play 90% of punk or rock music. It is easy to learn and feels very powerful to play loud. It is the perfect tool for when you feel that "agitated" energy building up.

3. Finding "The Others"

Since you mentioned potentially starting a band, you are in a great position.

  • The "Rhythm Section" Gap: You have the melody (piano) and the noise (guitar). To make it a full "high-intensity" experience, you essentially just need a drummer.
  • The Des Moines/Ankeny Scene: Des Moines has a surprisingly active underground music scene (punk, indie, metal). You don't need to be a pro to join a "jam." Many people are just looking for someone to make noise with in a garage.

A Challenge for the Week: Next time you feel that "wood being thrown on the fire" (stress or loss of control), instead of the usual ritual, try picking up the guitar or sitting at the piano. Don't try to play a "song." Just try to make a sound that matches the feeling.

Does the idea of making "noise" rather than "music" feel like it would help release that specific type of pressure?
